list.listitem: Measure weight, body mass index (BMI), and waist circumference and consider screening for thyroid disease, diabetes mellitus, and hyperlipidemia. C

Combined intervention of behavioral therapy along with low-calorie diet (500-1000 kcal/day deficit) and physical activity (30 minutes most days) provides the most successful therapy for weight loss and weight maintenance. A
Addition of appropriate weight loss medication to weight loss plan will produce more successful results in weight loss and weight maintenance. A
Bariatric surgery is effective but should be reserved for patients who have failed other strategies and have BMI >40 or BMI >35 with serious comorbidities. B

background.definition: Overweight is defined as BMI of 25 to 29.9 kg/m2; obesity is defined as a BMI >30 kg/m2 and morbid obesity is BMI >40 kg/m2.

list.listitem: Approximately 127 million adults in the United States are overweight, 60 million are obese (BMI >30), and 9 million are extremely obese (BMI >40).
Currently 64.5% of the US adults are overweight, 30.5% are obese, and 4.7% are severely obese.
It is estimated that the annual cost of diseases due to overweight and obesity in the United States is $122.9 billion.
The cost of lost productivity related to obesity among Americans age 17 to 64 is $3.9 billion.
Over $40 billion is spent every year by Americans on diet and dietary products.
Maternal obesity is associated with neural tube defects, structural anomalies (e.g., septal anomalies, cleft palate, limb reduction), and an increased risk of stillbirth.
Obesity is also a risk factor for urinary incontinence and weight loss can result in improvement.

Obesity (BMI >30) is a prognostic factor in identifying mortality risk in Covid-19 positive patient. A five-predictor risk prediction score (SOARS) based on demographic and clinical characteristics (includes obesity) can quickly and reliably identify COVID-19-positive patients who have a low probability of mortality for outpatient monitoring and management. A Cochrane review found higher mortality for COVID-19 patients with BMI ≥40 compared to patients with BMI <30 (OR 1.67, 95% CI 1.39 - 2.00, low certainty). Additionally, the odds of mechanical ventilation progressively increased with higher BMI, but rates of ICU admission and hospitalization did not appear to be associated with increasing BMI.
In a population-based study, increased body weight did not reduce total life expectancy in the older people but was associated with a higher risk of becoming and remaining disabled.
Overweight or obesity results when calorie intake exceeds calorie expenditure for an extended period of time.
There is now evidence to support that genetic, psychosocial, and environmental factors also play a role in development of obesity.

Overabundance of energy-dense food choices such as sweet drinks,community design that favors automobiles, and decreased opportunities and motivation for physical activity have greatly influenced American lifestyle patterns leading to overweight and obesity.
In the past decade research has shown that the brain plays a role in the regulation of food intake and pathogenesis of obesity.
The main area of brain that regulates energy homestasis is the hypothalamus, specifically the arcuate nucleus (ARC), paraventricular nucleus (PVN). Two types of neurons control food intake

Pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC): Stimulated by leptin (from fat) and insulin (from pancreas). Releases alpha-MSH (melanocyte stimulating hormone) which binds to MC4R, leading to reduction in appetite and increased energy expenditure.
Cocaine- and amphetamine-regulatin transcript (CART): Stimulated by anorexigenix neurons to suppress appetite. Believed to play role in award and addiction regulations.
Neuropeptide Y (NPY): Stimulated by gut hormone Ghrelin. Inhibited by leptin (from fat), insulin (from pancreas), serotonin (5-HT) and amylin.

Agouti-related peptide (AgRP): Stimulated by gut hormone Ghrelin. Inhibited by leptin (from fat), insulin (form pancreas), serotonin (5-HT) and amylin. Also highly expressed in the adrenal gland. Antagonizes alpha-MSH by competing with the alpha-MSH binding with MC4R which leads to lower satiety and overeating.
GI signaling—plays a role in homeostasis via mechano receptors and chemo sensors which detect the amount and quality of food intake.
Cholecytokinin (CCK)—released via duodenum and small intestine in response to fat and protein intake and signals satiety.
Peptide YY (PYY)—released in small intestine in response to luminal nutrient stumulation. It binds to and inactivated NPY/AgRP) leading to anorexia.
Glucagon-like-peptide-1 (GLP-1)—released in small intestine in response to luminal nutrient stimulaton. It delays gastric emptying leading to improved satiety.
Ghrelin—secreted from gut in response to meal, exerts an orexigenix effect. Its levels are elevated in fasting state ("hunger hormone").
Adipose signaling—adipose is an endocrine organ and secreted multiple hormone. Most important one is leptin.

Leptin—secreted by adipose tissue. The leptin levels correlate with adipose tissue mass. Leptin binds to ARC neuron and results in increased anorexigenic (POMC/CART) signaling and decreased activity of orexigenic signals (NPY/AgRP). Mose obese people have elevated leptin levels due to insensitivity to leptin.

Insulin—secreted from pancreatic B cells following a meal and transported to brain. Insulin binds to ARC neurons and results in POMC activation and NPY/AgRP inhibition, leading to reduced food intake. Obese people have insulin resistance.
The USPSTF recommends that clinicians screen all adult patients for obesity using the body mass index. B

The USPSTF also recommends providing or referring children and adolescents, 6 years or older, with a high BMI (at least 95th percentile for age and sex) to comprehensive, intensive behavioral interventions. Although the mean reduction in BMI with intervention was small (-0.7 compared with control), larger benefits occurred with more contact hours (> 26 total hours) that also offered physical activity sessions.
Offer intensive counseling and behavioral interventions to promote sustained weight loss for obese adults. B
Fiscal policy interventions such as taxation of sugar and fat contents in foods have uncertain effects on the primary prevention of obesity. B
Behavioral interventions aimed at health professionals and institutions to promote weight loss among patients with obesity or overweight have uncertain benefits in weight reduction. B
Implementation strategies to improve workplace interventions to modify obesity among employees have unclear benefits. B
The USPSTF recommends that clinicians screen all adult patients for obesity and offer intensive counseling and behavioral interventions to promote sustained weight loss for obese adults.
Recommend healthy lifestyle choices for physical activity and eating.
Fiscal policy interventions such as taxation of sugar and fat contents in foods have uncertain effects on obesity prevention.
Check body mass index (BMI) for all asymptomatic healthy patients.
Behavioral interventions aimed at health professionals and institutions to promote weight loss among patients with obesity or overweight have uncertain benefits in weight reduction.
Implementation strategies to improve workplace interventions to modify obesity among employees have unclear benefits.

Among patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD) and obesity (or overweight), all weight loss interventions have uncertain effects on mortality and morbidity. Nonsurgical interventions may reduce weight and improve LDL cholesterol, while surgical interventions may reduce weight, body fat, and waist circumference.
Measure weight, BMI, and waist circumference. C
Ask about comorbidities, diet, activity level, and previous attempts at weight loss. C
Strongly consider screening for thyroid disease, diabetes mellitus, hypertension and hyperlipidemia. C
See .
Weigh the patient, check the height, measure weight circumference, and calculate the patient's BMI.
Screen for depression, using a standard tool such as the PHQ9 screener. Review the patient's history for other comorbidities such as heart disease, diabetes mellitus, sleep apnea, and tobacco use.

Review the patient's current diet and beliefs around eating and food. A food diary can be helpful to provide insight to both patient and physician regarding food choices and calorie intake. Ask about exercise and activity level, and any previous weight loss attempts and diets.
Thyroid studies should be done to check for underlying thyroid disorder affecting metabolism and weight change.
Fasting blood sugar and a lipid profile should be ordered to assess for comorbidities.
Liver function tests should be ordered to assess for steatohepatitis.
Consider an ECG, especially if the patient will be joining a medical weight loss program and/or using appetite suppressants.
See and .
Weight loss should be about 1 to 2 pounds (0.5-1.0 kg) per week (calorie deficit of 500-1000 kcal/day) for a period of 6 months. B
All adults should set a long-term goal to accumulate at least 30 minutes or more of moderate-intensity physical activity on most and preferably all days of the week. B
Combined intervention of behavioral therapies along with low-calorie diet and physical activity provides the most successful therapy for weight loss and weight maintenance. A
There is no clear difference between low-fat, low-calorie, low-carbohydrate, and Mediterranean diets on weight loss or other outcomes. A
Pharmacotherapy can provide effective options for sustained weight loss, but some have cardiovascular and cancer risks. B
Bariatric surgery reduces all-cause mortality but should be reserved for patients who have failed other strategies and have BMI >40 or BMI >35 with serious comorbidities. B

In general, pharmacotherapy for weight loss is modestly effective in the short term and may improve some metabolic parameters such as blood sugar and lipid levels. Studies of long-term outcomes are lacking. Pharmacotherapy requires periodic monitoring by a physician.

Orlistat is somewhat effective in helping reduce weight when used in conjunction with weight-reducing diet. There was also a significant weight reduction with orlistat in people with defined obesity-related comorbidities such as type 2 diabetes mellitus, hyperlipidemia, or multiple cardiovascular risk factors compared with placebo.Common side effects are oily spotting, flatus, and fecal urgency.

Sibutramine, a centrally acting appetite suppressant that inhibits the reuptake of norepinephrine, dopamine, and serotonin, is minimally effective in promoting weight loss in obese people with or without obesity-related comorbidities.Most common side effects are tachycardia, dry mouth, and insomnia.This drug has been withdrawn from the US market (in October 2010) due to the risk of serious cardiovascular events.
Phentermine is moderately effective if used in conjunction with an exercise/diet program. Most common side effects are tachycardia, restlessness, and dizziness.
Rimonabant (Acomplia, not available in the United States), a cannabinoid-1 receptor blocker, is effective, but there is a significant risk for depression and other serious adverse events.

Lorcaserin (Belviq; FDA approved as of 2012) was voluntarily withdrawn from the US market at the request of the FDA in Feb. 2020 after a safety trial suggested it increased risk of cancer. In a cardiovascular safety trial, lorcaserin facilitated sustained weight loss without a higher rate of major cardiovascular events compared to placebo. In a study of 12,000 adults with vascular disease or T2DM and risk factors for CV disease, lorcaserin decreased the likelihood of progression to a diagnosis of T2DM (NNT = 57). There was also a greater likelihood of remission among patients with a diagnosis of T2DM.There was no difference in the rates of retinopathy or nephropathy.

Phentermine and extended release topiramate (FDA approved as of 2012; brand name Qsymia) has also shown promising results. Two-year SEQUEL trial showed a significant, sustained weight loss with this drug combination. Most common side effects include palpitation, dysgeusia, dry mouth, headache and insomnia.

Sustained release naltrexone and bupropion combination (FDA approved as of 2014; brand name Contrave) has also shown good weight loss. Four one-year clinical trials with more than 4500 patients showed modest weight loss. Patients who received Contrave and intensive behavior modification had even more weight loss. Eighty percent people getting contrave and intensive behavior modification lost more than 5% of weight and about fifty-five percent people lost about 10% of their weight. Most common side effects were nausea, constipation, headache and dizziness.

In December 2014, the FDA approved a glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonist, Liraglutide 3mg once-daily injection (brand name Saxenda), for chronic weight management. In the SCALE trial, the participants (n = 422) lost a mean 6.0% of screening weight during run-in. From randomization to week 56, weight decreased an additional mean 6.2% with liraglutide and 0.2% with placebo. More participants receiving liraglutide (81.4%) maintained the ≥5% run-in weight loss, compared with those receiving placebo (48.9%). Most common side effects were nausea and vomiting.

In 2021, the FDA approved the glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonist semaglutide 2.4mg (brand name Wegovy) as a once-weekly injection for chronic weight management. In the STEP 1 trial, the participants (n = 1306) lost a mean 14.9% in study group compared to 2.4% weight loss in placebo group after 68 weeks. In the SELECT trial, weekly semaglutide administered to patients 45 years and older with BMI ≥27 and established CV disease decreased body weight by around 9% and reduced the primary composite of CV death, nonfatal MI, or nonfatal stroke more than placebo (6.5% vs 8.0%; P < .001; NNT = 67 over 40 months). As secondary outcome, semaglutide reduced all-cause mortality more than placebo (4.3% vs 5.2%; P < .05; NNT = 111 over 40 months), but the researchers did not account for the possibility of type I errors due to multiple testing. The STEP-HFpEF Trial found that semaglutide given to nondiabetic, obese (BMI ≥30) patients with symptomatic HFpEF (≥45%) was more effective than placebo in improving heart failure symptoms, reducing body weight, and decreasing cardiac events.

In a RCT (n-2539) of middle-aged adults with a BMI > 30 or BMI > 27 and at least one weight-related complication, once-weekly tirzepatide 5 mg, 10 mg, and 15 mg injections reduced weight by 15%, 19.5%, and 20.9%, respectively, compared to 3.1% in a placebo injection group after 72 weeks.

Multiple systematic reviews and meta-analyses have found GLP-1 receptor agonists (e.g. semaglutide, liraglutide, tirzepatide, retatrutide) effective for weight loss in patients with overweight or obesity with or without diabetes, with weight loss ranging from 5 to 12 kg and 6% to 22% reduction in body weight. The most common adverse events were gastrointestinal (e.g. nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, decreased appetite) and were mild to moderate and nonpermanent. However, a recent cross-sectional study of data from NHANES pointed out that about one-third of people eligible for weight loss drugs are not represented in clinical research, meaning they've been excluded in clinical trials. These include patients with depression or severe psychiatric disorder, suicidal ideation, malignancy, liver disease (tirzepatide only), and uncontrolled hypertension. The authors recommended caution in using GLP-1 receptor agonists in this population given the lack of trial data.

Once weekly subcutaneous tirzepatide 10 mg or 15 mg leads to greater weight loss than once weekly subcutaneous semaglutide 1.7 mg or 2.4 mg in adults with obesity without diabetes. Other than effects on body weight, no other clinical outcomes were reported in this study. To date, no study has directly compared the highest dose of semaglutide (7.2 mg subcutaneous weekly) to tirzepatide 10 mg or 15 mg.
Aside from the subcutaneous route, oral semaglutide 25mg daily appears effective for weight loss in adults with overweight or obesity without diabetes (NNT = 2 for a 15% weight reduction).

Tirzepatide improves glycemic control in children and adolescents with type 2 diabetes and obesity, based on a small industry-sponsored RCT enrolling 99 children and adolescents (10 to 18 years of age). Additionally, participants treated with tirzepatide benefited from higher dose-dependent weight loss than those treated with placebo.

Canadian national guideline on pharmacotherapy to treat obesity recommend semaglutide, tirzepatide, liraglutide, naltrexone/bupropion, or orlistat for patients with BMI of at least 30 (or 27 with obesity-related complications). For specific comorbidities, semaglutide is recommended for patients with atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease; tirzepatide (preferred) or semaglutide is recommended for patients with heart failure; and liraglutide, orlistat, or tirzepatide is recommended for those with prediabetes. Tirzepatide or liraglutide is recommended for patients with sleep apnea, while semaglutide is recommended for those with osteoarthritis.

In an RCT, obese bipolar patients lost 4.2 kg with lamotrigine, gained 6.1 kg with lithium, and lost 0.6 kg with placebo.Another anticonvulsant, zonisamide (Zonegran), has been shown in small studies to facilitate weight loss, but long-term safety data are lacking.

A Cochrane review found low-certainty evidence that fluoxetine may be better than placebo in causing weight reduction, but low-certainty evidence also suggests higher adverse events (eg, nausea, drowsiness, dizziness, insomnia, fatigue).

A network meta-analysis of 32 unique trials involving 48,209 adults found phentermine-topiramate and GLP-1 receptor agonists to be the most effective pharmacologic treatments to achieve 5% weight loss for adults with overweight or obesity. The combination phentermine-topiramate was most effective (OR 8.02; 95% CI 5.24-12.27; mean weight loss 7.98%; NNT = 2), followed by GLP-1 receptor agonists (OR 6.33; 95% CI 5.00-8.00; mean weight loss 5.79%; NNT = 3). The likelihood of discontinuation due to adverse events were significant for both treatments (OR 2.40 for phentermine-topiramate, NNTH = 18; OR 2.22 for GLP-1 receptor agonists; NNTH = 20).

Bariatric surgery can be considered for people having BMI >40 or having BMI >35 with comorbidities. Surgery is more effective than conventional management with respect to weight loss, reduction in co-morbidities, and health-related quality of life up to 2 years; 10-year outcome differences are unclear. The risk and benefits of surgery should be carefully and thoroughly discussed with patient. Medical weight loss program and/or healthy lifestyle approach should be attempted first. Side effects can be significant.

A 10-year prospective nonrandomized clinical trial found that patients who chose bariatric surgery (BMI >34 kg/m2 for men and >38 kg/m2 for women) experienced a reduction in all-cause mortality (5.0 vs. 6.3%, NNT = 77 to prevent 1 death at 10 years). Weight loss at 10 years was 14% for banding, 16% for vertical banded gastroplasty, and 25% for gastric bypass. The same study also demonstrated a lower number of cardiovascular deaths and first-time cardiovascular events (myocardial infarction or stroke) in the bariatric sugery group.

In a trial of 150 adults with a body mass index between 27 and 43 and hemoglobin A1c >7.0%, participants randomized to bariatric surgery plus intensive medical therapy had better weight and glycemic control, less use of glucose-lowering medications, and improved quality of life compared to participants assigned to medical therapy only.
The likelihood of having diabetes and hypertension is also decreased for very obese patients who have bariatric surgery.

Gastric bypass surgery results in greater weight loss compared to gastric banding. Patients treated with laparoscopic adjustable gastric banding had lower short-term morbidity than those treated with Roux-en-Y gastric bypass, but reoperation rates were higher among patients who received laparoscopic adjustable gastric banding.

Studies of alternative therapies (ayurvedic herbal preparations, chitosan, chromium picolinate, ephedra, guar gum, and Garcinia cambogia)have generally been of low quality and short duration. None can be confidently recommended with regards to efficacy and safety.

Ephedra and ephedrine can promote modest weight loss, but there are serious risks including death and major disability occurring in up to 1 in 1000 users, and it should not be recommended.Ephedra is currently banned throughout the United States.
Acupoint embedment, a modified acupuncture technique, has shown effectiveness in reducing BMI and mean body weight compared to placebo in a meta-analysis.

Physical activity should be an integral part of weight loss therapy and weight maintenance. Initially moderate levels of physical activity for 30 to 45 minutes, 3 to 5 days per week, should be encouraged.
All adults should set a long-term goal to accumulate at least 30 minutes or more of moderate-intensity physical activity on most, and preferably all, days of the week.
Using a pedometer can result in modest weight loss.Your goal should be to walk about 10,000 steps daily.

Behavior therapy strategies to promote diet and physical activity should be used routinely, as they are highly helpful in achieving weight loss. The bulk of the evidence supports the use of behavioral and cognitive-behavioral strategies. Other psychological interventions are less rigorously evaluated for their efficacy as weight loss treatments. There is no conclusive evidence that incorporating the Transtheoretical Model into interventions leads to sustainable weight loss.
These strategies include self-monitoring of eating habits and physical activity, stress management, stimulus control, contingency management, cognitive restructuring, and social support.

Initial goal of weight loss therapy should be to reduce body weight by approximately 10% over 6 months. Weight loss should be about 1 to 2 lb/week (calorie deficiency of 500-1000 kcal/day) for a period of 6 months.

Financial incentives were not found to be better than monthly weigh-in for promoting weight loss. Interventions aimed at health care professionals such as educating them and encouraging dietician referral showed some benefit in studies of modest quality.

Weight maintenance program should be a priority after the initial 6 month of weight loss. E-mail based counseling can be effective. Monthly brief personal contact can also provide modest benefit in sustaining weight loss after participation in a weight loss program.

After successful weight loss, the likelihood of weight loss maintenance is enhanced by a program consisting of dietary therapy, physical activity, and behavior therapy, which should be continued indefinitely. Drug therapy can also be used. However, drug safety and efficacy beyond 1 year of total treatment have not been established.

A low-calorie diet (LCD) consisting of 800 to 1500 kcal/day is recommended instead of very low-calorie diet (VLCD) consisting of 250 to 800 kcal/day because the deficits are too great and nutritional inadequacies will occur unless VLCD is supplemented with vitamins and minerals. Most of the newer VLCD products are fortified with vitamin and minerals and produce significant weight loss with less side effects when monitored weekly by a physician. LCD are just as effective as VLCDs in producing weight loss after 1 year.There is no difference between low-fat and low-calorie diets in terms of final weight loss.
In a RCT of 4 low calorie diets (differing in the content of fat, protein and carbohydrates) all produced clinically significant weight loss and there were no differences between them.

A Cochrane review found little to no difference between low-carbohydrate and balanced-carbohydrate diets in reducing wieght and cardiovascular risk among patients with overweight or obesity, with or without type 2 diabetes.

A Cochrane review found little to no difference between low glycemic index or glycemic load diets compared to higher glycemic index or glycemic load diets or any other diet when it comes to improving body weight, BMI, health-related quality of life, and mortality.
Two RCTs comparing the Mediterranean diet, a low-fat diet, and a low-carbohydrate diet found similar outcomes in terms of weight loss and impact on metabolic profiles.
A meta-analysis of 5 studies with 447 people (3 following patients for up to 1 year) had similar findings of equivalency between low-fat and low-carbohydrate diets.

A Cochrane review found small but consistent evidence of efficacy in low-fat diet over a high-fat diet in patients not intentionally aiming to lose weight. Patients on a low-fat diet appear to have lower weight, BMI, percentage body fat, and waist circumference compared to those on a high-fat diet.
In a systematic review of workplace interventions, worksite nutrition and physical activity programs achieved modest improvements in employee weight status (−2.8 pounds) at 6- to 12-month follow-up.
A Cochrane review found limited evidence and a lack of clear benefit from behavioral interventions using mobile health apps and wearables for adolescents and adults with obesity or overweight.
Patient should have follow-up visit monthly for 3 months, and then every 3 months for a year to monitor weight loss and weight maintenance using BMI and waist circumference. C
Body Mass Index (BMI) combined with Waist-to-Hip Ratio (WHR) offers the best predictability for mortality or CVD in middle-aged and older-aged adults.A
Obesity is associated with a slightly higher rate of infectious complications from knee and hip replacement surgery, but does not increase risk for venous thromboembolism. B

GLP-1 receptor agonists are associated with a lower risk of obesity-related cancer than other glucose-lowering drugs in adults with overweight or obesity with type 2 diabetes, based on a large population-based cohort study. B

In a randomized controlled trial of 107 frail obese adults over 65 years of age, a combination of exercise and weight management was more effective than exercise and weight management alone at improving weight loss and physical performance.
Combination of resistance and aerobic exercise are best for obese elderly patients.
Although the quality and quantity of evidence on weight loss interventions in the elderly is limited, they appear to result in modest weight loss and improved function.
Interventions to improve sedentary lifestyle among community-dwelling older adults have uncertain benefits.
Obese women are more likely to develop diabetes, hypertension, preeclampsia, and arrest of labor; however, these were not affected by gestational weight gain.

No weight loss should be recommended during pregnancy. However, reduced weight gain is recommended in very overweight women during pregnancy, although the literature to support this recommendation is weak.
Pregnancy after gastric banding appears to be safe, based on a prospective cohort study of 79 women.

A meta-analysis of 20 cohort studies of pregnancy outcomes after bariatric surgery found that benefits included less gestational diabetes, maternal hypertension, cesarean deliveries, and large-for-gestational age infants; harms included more preterm deliveries and small-for-gestational age infants.
Antenatal administration of metformin in obese pregnant women without diabetes resulted in reduced maternal weight gain but not neonatal birth weight.
Children of mothers treated for gestational diabetes (GDM) had similar rates of obesity at 3 to 7 years of age as children of mothers without GDM, based on a cohort study in New Zealand.
A Cochrane systematic review concluded that behavioral lifestyle interventions are effective fo weight loss in obese adolescents and children.

The USPSTF recommends providing or referring children and adolescents, 6 years or older, with a high BMI (at least 95th percentile for age and sex) to comprehensive, intensive behavioral interventions. Although the mean reduction in BMI with intervention was small (-0.7 compared with control), larger benefits occurred with more contact hours (> 26 total hours) that also offered physical activity sessions.
At least 60 minutes of moderate to vigorous physical activity are recommended for children.
An intensive intervention of diet, behavioral counseling, and physical activity is effective for children, with a 6 kg weight loss compared to controls over 1 year.

The role of the physician in providing intervention and monitoring for overweight children is not supported in one study. The intervention included four standard consultations over 12 weeks targeting change in nutrition, physical activity, and sedentary behavior and included written support materials. There were no differences between intervention and control groups in physical activity, nutrition, or BMI at 6 and 12 months.

In a small randomized crossover study (n = 28) of adolescents with insulin resistance, those randomized to metformin 1 g twice daily lost 4.35 kg more than those taking placebo over a 6-month period.Other studies have found minimal effects of metformin on BMI in overweight children. Long-term benefit and risks are uncertain, so this is not routinely recommended at this time.
Orlistat was studied in 539 obese adolescents and was found to reduce the amount of weight gained over 1 year (1.2 pounds vs. 6.9 pounds).

Liraglutide at a targeted dose of 3 mg subcutaneously daily in children 6 to 11 years of age appears more effective than placebo after 1 year in reducing BMI (5.8% lower) and decreasing weight gain (6 kg lower). Adverse events were primarily gastrointestinal and led to a drop out rate of 11% for luraglutide, compared to none for the placebo group.
